title: What Good Readers Know
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: Robert Pondiscio uses Richard Feynman's image of the Pacific Island cargo cults to diagnose a long-running error in American reading instruction: teaching struggling readers to imitate the visible behaviors of good readers (asking questions, making connections, predicting) while neglecting the invisible infrastructure of vocabulary and background knowledge that actually makes comprehension possible. Drawing on his years teaching fifth grade in the South Bronx, he distinguishes decoding, a genuinely transferable skill, from comprehension, which is inseparable from what the reader already knows. He marshals Hirsch's cultural literacy, the Recht and Leslie baseball study, and Stanovich's Matthew effects to argue that knowledge compounds, so children who start with less fall further behind. The essay then extends the argument to critical thinking and 'thinking like a historian,' insisting that expert thinking cannot be separated from expert knowledge. Its practical move is to reframe comprehension as a condition schools create rather than a skill they teach, and to place responsibility for a cumulative, knowledge-rich curriculum on principals, districts, and state leaders rather than on individual teachers alone.
points: Comprehension strategy posters and think-alouds amount to 'cargo-cult reading': they copy what fluent readers visibly do while ignoring the vocabulary and background knowledge doing the real work beneath the surface.

The Recht and Leslie baseball study showed that 'poor readers' who knew baseball outperformed 'good readers' who did not, undercutting the idea that comprehension is a subject-neutral transferable skill.
Knowledge compounds through incidental vocabulary learning, so the Matthew effect widens gaps: children with more knowledge extract more from every lesson and text.
Every hour spent drilling main idea and author's purpose is an hour lost from science, history, and the arts, which Pondiscio argues are the actual means by which literacy develops.
Because a knowledge-rich curriculum must build cumulatively across years, the decisive levers sit with principals, district curriculum choices, and state standards, not with individual teachers.
quotes: None of this is visible in the way that asking a question, making a prediction, or stopping to summarize is visible. And therein lies the fatal instructional mistake that has held back reading achievement for decades: We observed what good readers do and tried to teach struggling readers to imitate those behaviors, while paying far less attention to what good readers know.
Students judged to be “poor readers” who knew a lot about baseball substantially outperformed ostensibly “good readers” who knew little about the game.
It’s not quite right to say that background knowledge improves reading comprehension. That makes knowledge sound like an enhancement—a helpful supplement that makes reading somewhat easier.

Two children can sit through the same lesson or read the same book and emerge having learned different amounts—not because one is more intelligent or attentive, but because one had more knowledge available to make sense of the new material.

This is why the familiar conflict between teaching knowledge and teaching children “how to think” is misconceived. Knowledge does not crowd out higher-order thinking. It’s what makes higher-order thinking possible.

Every additional hour spent practicing finding the main idea, making connections, and identifying an author’s purpose is an hour that is lost learning about the solar system, ancient civilizations, ecosystems, mythology, music, art, and literature—the knowledge that will make future texts more comprehensible.

If knowledge compounds, then a genuinely knowledge-rich education must compound too. A coherent curriculum should build deliberately and cumulatively from year to year. No individual teacher can create that coherence alone.
Reading comprehension is not principally a skill we teach. It is a condition we create. And we create it by teaching children about the world.
